entry.title: Rising from the valley: a new sustainable woodland centre takes shape at Yarner Wood
entry.summary: By Chris Harbut, Reserve Manager, Devon National Nature Reserves Tucked into a steep-sided Dartmoor valley, a new woodland centre is taking shape at Yarner Wood, built almost entirely from timber grown in the surrounding landscape. In this post, we share …
entry.content:
By Chris Harbut, Reserve Manager, Devon National Nature Reserves

Tucked into a steep-sided Dartmoor valley, a new woodland centre is taking shape at Yarner Wood, built almost entirely from timber grown in the surrounding landscape. In this post, we share how the building is coming together, from the Douglas fir frame to the cedar cladding still to come. We also explain how sustainability has shaped every decision, including the off-grid power and water systems, and how we hope the centre will welcome schools, community groups and partners when it opens at the end of the year.

If you've visited Yarner Wood recently, you may have noticed something new rising among the trees. Tucked into this steep-sided Dartmoor valley, within the East Dartmoor National Nature Reserve (NNR), a new woodland centre is taking shape. One built almost entirely from timber sourced from the surrounding landscape. We wanted to share the story of how it's coming together, and why sustainability is at the very heart of this project.

Construction of this new, purpose-built facility, will replace the previous woodland centre. Work began earlier this year, and since then it's been a hive of activity here at Yarner. Following the initial site clearance and logistics work, the timber frame has been erected, the roof is on, windows are being installed, and cladding is being put on.

This is no standard facility, but a considered response to its unique landscape setting, with generous natural light and a strong sense of place designed to keep visitors connected to the woodland around them at every turn.

A building made from the woodland it sits within

The timber is the star of this project. The building's frame, now proudly standing tall, is built from beams crafted from Douglas fir donated by the Woodland Trust. The timber was sourced from within the NNR, from Plantations on Ancient Woodland Sites (PAWS). This is ongoing woodland restoration work that is transitioning conifer plantations on ancient woodland sites back to native deciduous woodland and temperate rainforest. Use of this material directly links the building to ongoing landscape restoration efforts.

That story will continue over the coming weeks. Once the windows are fitted, exterior cladding will go on, predominantly using western red cedar, also supplied by the Woodland Trust. This timber is naturally durable and oily, requiring minimal treatment to stay weatherproof, further reducing the building's long-term environmental impact and maintenance needs.

Sustainability at the core

As the building sits entirely within the NNR , sustainability and environmental sensitivity have shaped every part of the project.

The facility will operate fully off-grid. Water will be supplied through rainwater harvesting and, where appropriate, the adjacent stream. Solar panels will feed a substantial battery storage system, with approximately 30 kVA of capacity, significantly reducing reliance on fossil fuels and allowing the building to run silently for much of the year.

Due to the building's location in a steep-sided, wooded Dartmoor valley, power generation can be limited during periods of low sunlight, particularly in winter. As a result, a generator will remain part of the energy system, although it has been relocated further from the building and will be used far less frequently. The battery system ensures that low-level power demands, such as lighting, no longer require the generator to run continuously. During summer months, generator use is unlikely to be needed.

Heating will be provided primarily by a gasification boiler rather than electric systems. Combined with exceptionally high levels of insulation, this means the building will need very little energy input to stay comfortable year-round. While not formally certified as a passive building, it has been designed to perform close to passive standards within practical and budgetary constraints.

Looking ahead

Once finished, the new centre will play a key role in supporting engagement, events and activities, having been designed specifically to enable and promote this kind of activity.

The old woodland centre has long been a hub for the local community, with schools, universities and student nurses among those who have used the space over the years. We want to build on that success.

As the new centre takes shape, we're keen to work with local organisations, partners across the sector, and community groups to explore additional uses and reach new people.

If you'd like to be part of that conversation we'd love to hear from you, so do get in touch. Keep an eye on the East Dartmoor NNR social channels for more updates as the building work heads towards completion at the end of the year.

entry.title: Showing up together: why good health starts long before you reach a hospital
entry.summary: Earlier this month, national bodies including Natural England, Sport England, Arts Council England and NHS England met at the Cabinet Office to ask how they can work together to support local leaders in creating the conditions for good health. Read this post to find out more.
entry.content:
By Oliver Harmar, Natural England's Chief Strategy Officer 

Leaders from national bodies including Natural England, Sport England and NHS England met at the Cabinet Office to explore how to work together to support healthier places. Oliver Harmer reflects on the 20-year gap in healthy life expectancy, a joined-up approach being tested in the West Midlands, and why good health is created in the "gloriously ordinary" parts of everyday life.

Earlier this month, I had the privilege of chairing a meeting hosted by the Cabinet Office that felt different from most I attend in government. 

Around the table were leaders from across government: Natural England, Active Travel England, Sport England, Arts Council England, Historic England, NHS England, Homes England, West Midlands Combined Authority, and the Cabinet Office's Test, Learn and Grow team.  

The question we had come together to answer was simple to ask, but hard to answer: how do we better align nationally, so we can show up together and support local leaders to create the conditions for good health? 

It’s a crucial question, because if you live in one of the least deprived areas of England, you can expect to spend around 20 more years in good health than someone living in one of the most deprived areas. That’s a shocking gap that should motivate us all to act. 

We know that health isn't just created in hospitals and GP surgeries. Health outcomes are shaped upstream by factors such as housing, income, transport, physical inactivity and people's wider environment, while the NHS and healthcare often deals with the eventual consequences of ill health. It's created in the parks, libraries, cycle lanes, nature, community choirs, museums, football clubs, the home you live in and the street you walk down.  

Each of our organisations already has big ambitions in this space. Natural England helps people access green spaces that lift mental and physical wellbeing, supporting our strategy’s ambition to deliver nature recovery as a foundation for the nation’s growth, health and security. Active Travel England makes it easier and safer for children to walk or cycle to school. Sport England seeks to tackle stubborn inequalities that exist in sport and physical activity by removing the barriers that prevent people, particularly those with the most to gain, from taking part. Arts Council England puts creativity at the heart of healthier communities. Historic England shows how heritage and belonging support happiness and connection.  Homes England creates healthier communities through quality housing and well-designed places.  

But here's the challenge we set ourselves: too often we work alongside each other, rather than truly with each other. So, we want to test a new way of working together in the West Midlands to find out what it really looks like when national bodies show up as one team in service of a place.  This will explore questions over joint governance, shared outcome metrics, how to work across organisational boundaries and how activity can connect at national, regional and neighbourhood levels.  

We want to be open about what we're learning, including what doesn't work, so other places can learn with us from the start. We know that what works in one place might not be the thing that’s needed in another but hope that we can develop a repeatable model for how ALBs work collectively in places. At its core will be a more joined up approach that listens to place-leaders so that we can all work more effectively together to support healthier households, communities and neighbourhoods across the country. 

Ultimately, this is about enabling us all the “gloriously ordinary” things that enrich our lives - a walk in nature, a trip to a local museum, a safe cycle to school, a seat in a community choir.  These everyday activities are where good health is created.

entry.title: Tony Juniper: COP17, From Promises to Implementation

category.term: United Nations Convention on Biological Diversity

entry.summary: As the 17th Convention on Biological Diversity COP gets underway in Armenia, Tony Juniper, Chair of Natural England, reflects on what's really at stake behind the headlines, technical reports and policy jargon: a global commitment made in 2022 to halt …
entry.content:
As the 17th Convention on Biological Diversity COP gets underway in Armenia, Tony Juniper, Chair of Natural England, reflects on what's really at stake behind the headlines, technical reports and policy jargon: a global commitment made in 2022 to halt and reverse Nature's decline by 2030, and the uncomfortable truth that progress so far, in the UK and elsewhere, is falling short. In this blog, he looks at where things stand at the halfway point to 2030, what Natural England is doing to help close the gap, and why recovering Nature must be seen not as a brake on growth, but as the foundation for it.

The 17th conference of the parties (COP) of the United Nations Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD) is underway in Armenia. As usual, much jargon, technical content and specialist reports will be in circulation, as countries wrestle with the historic task of halting Nature’s decline, and embarking on the process of nurturing its recovery.

Despite all the complexity of science, policy and law under discussion, however, there is one simple truth at the heart of this global gathering. This is the fact of Nature being in catastrophic decline, with risks to the whole world as the web of life that sustains us is progressively and rapidly torn apart. Governments attending this meeting can have no doubt that the stakes are high, and the need for decisive action urgent.

Prominent on the agenda will be review of progress toward meeting the aims of the Global Biodiversity Framework (GBF) agreed in Montreal in 2022 at the 15th COP of the CBD. Back then nearly every country on Earth agreed to a programme that would reverse historic losses, via pursuit of 23 targets set against four longer term goals. The date for delivering this ambitious programme was set at 2030, with the Armenia meeting thus marking the halfway point between adoption and delivery of the GBF. 

As we enter this important stock-taking moment, those paying attention to the seemingly endless procession of reports which document the continuing decline of Nature will not be surprised to know that we are not where we need to be. Of the countries that have submitted progress reports (all of them should have done, but many have not) there is a consistent pattern of patchy delivery, with most of the outcomes agreed in 2022 way off target for delivery. Perhaps we should not be surprised that these stretching goals are proving difficult to reach, given the long-term nature of environmental decline and the severe global difficulties arising from war and economic pressures. But recovering Nature isn’t really optional, and failing to grasp the nettle now only makes it much more expensive to do so further down the line.

A renewed sense of urgency is required if we are to avoid further loss of natural diversity, ecosystem degradation and complete collapse of some wildlife populations. This is not only because many people care about beautiful animals and plants, but because our human life support system is at risk too. All our food, water and even the air we breathe originates in healthy natural systems, and the more we degrade those the more we imperil our own wellbeing.

Closing this gap between progress and ambition will not be easy with the targets in the GBF all presenting significant challenges. For example, back in 2022 we and more than 200 other countries agreed to protect 30 per cent of land and sea for Nature by 2030. We said we’d halt extinctions, restore 30 per cent of degraded land and make steps toward sustainable consumption patterns. We said we’d take action to cut pollution, including reducing the risks posed by pesticides and fertilisers by half and that we’d integrate biodiversity across all policy areas. All this and more has gone too slowly, and the UK is not alone. As we grapple with this rather troubling global context at the COP meetings, it is very important to remember that it is the work done within countries that will make the difference in meeting the 2030 targets. 

This is of course of great interest to all of us at Natural England as we look at what we can do to help, including through the host of partnerships now underway which strive to restore Nature at scale. For example, The King’s of Series of National Nature Reserves is on target to create or extend 25 NNRs between 2023 and 2028. It has already brought many thousands of hectares of additional land into Nature recovery and brought 1.4 million people closer to the natural world, including in many areas suffering aspects of social deprivation. We are beginning to look at how we might capitalise on this successful programme in the years beyond 2028.

When it comes to reducing the risk of species going extinct in our islands our Species Recovery Programme continues to make a significant positive impact. Between 2022 and 2024 it supported action for the conservation and recovery of 600 species and with a further £60 million being invested over the next 3 years, water voles, chough, adders and salmon are among the many more species set to benefit from targeted action. 

On the complex challenge of reducing pollution we have also worked with a number of local authorities, developers and other organisations to reduce the impact on our most sensitive Nature sites, enabling thousands of new homes to be built – an approach we are now taking forward with the first Environmental Delivery Plan in Norfolk.

Despite these and other important examples of collaboration, though, as a nation our trajectory towards 2030 isn’t where it needs to be. If we can’t succeed in bending the curve in the UK, it would be unfair to expect anything different from Indonesia, Brazil, Democratic Republic of Congo and other countries with enviably vast biodiversity, including rainforests, rivers, mountains and grasslands. If on the other hand we can get firmly on the path toward Nature recovery, with all the pressures we must grapple with on land and sea, then we might truly claim to be leaders, and in so doing inspire others.

As we observe and measure that gap between ambition and progress it is important to ask why this is all proving so difficult. One thing that I would say is a major factor is the continuing misconception that recovering Nature is hostile to economic growth. Many still see looking after our life support system as a distraction, an unaffordable expense or a series of unnecessary regulatory barriers, even when a vast body of evidence reveals the direct opposite to be the case.

In recognition of this rather fundamental barrier, last year Natural England  launched a new strategy called Recovering Nature For Growth, Health And Security. We are very confident about the linkages between Nature and a thriving human world and are working across government to find the ways in which we can recover Nature to enable growth, promote wellbeing and assist with national resilience in ways that will help meet the 2022 GBF targets. Making Nature recovery central to the creation of new homes, infrastructure and communities – and vice versa – is the best way of meeting a host of essential priorities in a cost-effective way, building our nation’s resilience in the process. Greater collaboration involving government, business, communities and NGOs really can move us closer to our targets.

That wider collaboration is gathering momentum with a multitude of partners now involved, including through the new Government-led National Estate for Nature. This brings together a wide group of landowners from NGOs to government agencies and from private estates to the Church in making bigger plans of Nature and adding more land toward the 2030 target. Private finance is beginning to come into Nature's recovery and progress on the ground is revealing the speed at which she can recover, if given a chance, and where needed a helping hand.

None of this is easy, but as we mark another global COP it is important to remember that it is at home in multiple countries that the difference will in the end be made. Are we up for being leaders, or do we think protecting the web of life is too expensive, inconvenient and complicated?

entry.title: Transforming towns and cities for people and nature
entry.summary: By Chloe Fay, Principal Officer for Urban Greening and Nature Towns and Cities Nature Towns and Cities is a UK-wide movement helping urban areas become greener, healthier and more connected to nature. Recent learning events in Sunderland and Bristol brought …
entry.content:
By Chloe Fay, Principal Officer for Urban Greening and Nature Towns and Cities

Nature Towns and Cities is a UK-wide movement helping urban areas become greener, healthier and more connected to nature. Recent learning events in Sunderland and Bristol brought local authorities, communities and partners together to share ideas and visit local projects, from regenerated green spaces to community-led "Greening Permits". Read on to see how both cities are turning ambition into action, and what it means for the programme's goal of improving green space for 10 million people over the next decade.

How can we put nature at the heart of the places where people live, work and spend their everyday lives? That ambition sits at the centre of Nature Towns and Cities, a growing movement helping make urban areas greener, healthier and more connected to the natural world.

Founded by The National Lottery Heritage Fund, Natural England and the National Trust, the programme supports towns and cities across the UK to create places where people and nature can thrive together.

Recent learning events in Sunderland and Bristol offered a glimpse of what this looks like in practice. Local authorities, voluntary organisations and delivery partners shared ideas, reflected on challenges and explored practical solutions. Discussions ranged from green finance and partnership governance to tree equity and public engagement, while site visits showcased inspiring local projects and thriving green and blue spaces.

Natural England was represented at both events, with Chief Strategy Officer Oliver Harmar attending in Sunderland and our new Chief Executive, Neil Hornby, joining partners in Bristol. Together, the events demonstrated the enthusiasm, creativity and commitment helping turn ambition into action across the Nature Towns and Cities network.

Sunderland: nature and pride in place

In Sunderland, local authorities, partners and community organisations highlighted how investment in nature can support regeneration and strengthen pride in place.

Supported by a £490,000 grant from The National Lottery Heritage Fund through Nature Towns and Cities, Sunderland is creating more opportunities for residents to experience and shape their local natural environment while building on the city's distinctive identity.

Its shipbuilding and mining heritage remains central to its story. Alongside it, nature recovery, public realm improvements and community spaces are helping create places that celebrate Sunderland's past while looking confidently to its future.

Visits to Copt Hill, King George V Park and Flint Mill brought that change to life. At Copt Hill, a once-overlooked landscape has become an inviting green space, while King George V Park is attracting visitors and supporting a thriving local café. At Flint Mill, habitat improvements and better access are helping people enjoy the environment on their doorstep.

The common thread was people. These projects are not simply improving landscapes; they are helping local neighbourhoods rediscover and reconnect with the places around them. Reflecting on the visit, Natural England's Chief Officer for Strategy, Oliver Harmar, said: “It has been brilliant over the last year and a half to see Nature Towns and Cities growing from strength to strength. While this may be a national initiative, what I saw in Sunderland were inspiring examples of local leadership and innovation, all focused on bringing the benefits of nature and green space to those who need them most.”

Bristol: empowering communities to act

In Bristol, our new Chief Executive, Neil Hornby, joined partners to see a different approach to bringing nature closer to people. Supported by a £984,126 grant from The National Lottery Heritage Fund through Nature Towns and Cities, Bristol's Nature Together project is transforming how the city works with partners and communities to support local action for nature.

One innovation is the Greening Permit, a simple scheme that enables residents and community groups to create small-scale nature projects in council-owned green spaces, such as planters, wildflower areas and tree planting. By streamlining permissions, it helps communities turn ideas into action while supporting neighbourhood nature planning and strengthening volunteering, community leadership and ecological expertise across the city.

Visits to Lockleaze, The Ardagh and Horfield Common demonstrated what collaboration can achieve when local people have the support and opportunity to shape their green spaces. The events were also about learning from each other. People from different towns, cities and organisations came together to discuss successes, challenges and new approaches, generating ideas that can travel between places.

Growing a movement for urban nature

Sunderland and Bristol are different cities with different opportunities, but both demonstrate the value of bringing local authorities, partners and residents together around nature. For Natural England, being part of Nature Towns and Cities means contributing expertise and partnerships to that collective effort, while also listening and learning from the places already making change happen.

Nature Towns and Cities has an ambition to improve neighbourhood green space for 10 million people over the next decade. With the partnership continuing to grow and more places sharing their knowledge and experience, Sunderland and Bristol offer an exciting glimpse of what's possible when nature is woven into the fabric of everyday life. Through greener neighbourhoods, stronger local connections and better access to nature, the programme is bringing to fruition Natural England’s strategic aim to build nature into everyday life for more people in towns and cities across the country.

Find out more on the Nature Towns and Cities website.

entry.title: Have your say: A closer look at Norfolk’s Environmental Delivery Plan
entry.summary: By Brad Tooze, Director, Nature Restoration Fund The Nature Restoration Fund provides a new way to support development while delivering larger-scale improvement for nature. It focusses on achieving an overall benefit for nature, rather than maintaining the status quo. The …
entry.content:
By Brad Tooze, Director, Nature Restoration Fund

The Nature Restoration Fund provides a new way to support development while delivering larger-scale improvement for nature. It focusses on achieving an overall benefit for nature, rather than maintaining the status quo.

The first Environmental Delivery Plan (EDP) in England will focus on the impact of nitrogen and phosphorous, otherwise known as nutrient pollution, and has been developed to protect and enhance the Norfolk Broads and River Wensum Special Areas of Conservation and Broadland Ramsar. Following work with local stakeholders, Norfolk’s draft plan is currently going through public consultation, giving you the opportunity to help shape the final approach.

The wider context

The Norfolk Broads and River Wensum have been affected by nutrient pollution for many years, with pollution coming from a range of sources. New development alone did not create these historic problems, and its contribution is relatively small compared with the wider pressures on the water environment.

These wider water quality issues are being addressed through other government and industry action, with significant investments, and the government has announced a commitment to a Water Bill. 

 What will the EDP do?

The EDP will leave the habitats and species impacted by new development in a better position than they would be in a world than where the EDP (and its associated development and conservation measures) did not exist.

Under the alternative nutrient neutrality system, developments affecting protected sites have to demonstrate that they will not increase nutrient pollution. This is usually achieved by purchasing nutrient credits, which offsets the additional pollution generated by development.

Under this EDP we have proposed a series of measures which will work in combination to deliver real benefits for the identified habitats and species. This includes removing nutrients created by development whilst also supporting wider, lasting improvements to habitat extent, connectivity and quality.

An example of how we have sought to deliver multiple benefits is removing nutrient inputs on land at the same time as improving its environmental quality by changing land use from intensive forms of agriculture to semi-natural habitats. These can also be positioned next to existing and new high-quality areas (including fen creation), improving environmental resilience. Because of the range and scale of pressures on the habitats and species, we need to put in place a package of measures that will both remove nutrients and deliver wider benefits to result in a material improvement which is the key legal test.

The science and evidence behind conservation measures

Natural England undertook an evidence review to investigate the effectiveness of the conservation measures considered for inclusion in the EDP. This review gathered information on environmental benefits, as well as requirements for the measure to be effective (e.g.  location or long-term maintenance needs), time to effectiveness, and potential environmental risks.

Conservation measures were shortlisted by assessing each potential measure against a set of criteria including those relating to delivery, the strength of evidence for their effectiveness, and their potential to deliver a range of environmental benefits suitable for the local area. The approach taken to assess the strength of evidence was recommended in a policy brief produced by researchers at Oxford University (Stuart et al. 2026)).

The approach to conservation measure selection in the EDP was also scrutinised by Defra scientists and external members of Defra’s Biodiversity Expert Committee. 

How the Overall Improvement Test works, including the safeguards built into the NRF

This is not a one-off test, but an ongoing commitment by Natural England over at least the lifetime of the EDP, keeping nature at the forefront.

Monitoring and reporting will track delivery, backed by remedial action, back-up measures and powers to amend or revoke an EDP if it is not delivering as expected.

Don’t miss your chance to shape the final EDP

This is a new approach under new legislation, and your feedback matters.

Responses through this consultation will directly inform the final design and approaches helping to ensure the Nature Restoration Fund is practical, proportionate and effective.

A Business Readiness Forum was held on 21 September to walk-through the draft EDP and host an extended Q&A session. You can watch this back on our YouTube channel, and we have a write-up of all questions raised during the Q&A.

 How to share your views

Please respond to this consultation in one of the following ways:

1. Online using the Smart Survey consultation hub.

For ease of analysis, responses via the Smart Survey platform would be preferred, but alternative options are provided below, if required:

2. By email to: nrfconsultations@naturalengland.org.uk

Please use the word document titled ‘Consultation questions on draft Environmental Delivery Plan – Nutrient Pollution – Norfolk’ on Smart Survey to complete your responses before sending to the email address above.

3. By post:

EDP Consultation Team
Natural England
Foss House,
Kings Pool
1-2 Peasholme Green
York
YO1 7PX

Please use the word document titled ‘Consultation questions on draft Environmental Delivery Plan – Nutrient Pollution – Norfolk’ on Smart Survey to complete your responses before sending to the postal address above.

Please note, any responses sent by post must have arrived at the above address by the closing time.

Natural England will consider the feedback from the consultation before finalising the EDP.  All consultation responses will be provided to the Secretary of State. The closing date for responses is Tuesday 27 October (9.29am).

entry.title: Why I brought Europe's infrastructure and nature network to Bristol
entry.summary: The Infrastructure and Ecology Network Europe came to the UK for the first time this September, marking its 30th anniversary. Louise McGowan reflects on bringing the conference to Bristol, lessons from colleagues in more than 40 countries, and why nature must be regarded as infrastructure.
entry.content:
By Louise McGowan, Principal Adviser for Nature-based Solutions and Climate Change, Natural England, and Conference Chair, IENE 2026 

The Infrastructure and Ecology Network Europe came to the UK for the first time this September, marking its 30th anniversary. Louise McGowan reflects on bringing the conference to Bristol, lessons from colleagues in more than 40 countries, and why nature must be regarded as infrastructure.

In September, the Infrastructure and Ecology Network Europe (IENE) came to the UK for the first time, marking 30 years of bringing transport and nature together. Nearly 300 delegates from more than 40 countries spent 5 days in Bristol exploring how we build infrastructure that works for both people and nature. For many UK delegates, it was their first encounter with a community they didn't know existed. 

"What an incredible community. I'd never heard of it before."  

A delegate said to me halfway through the week, and others told me much the same. For me, this was validation that bringing IENE to the UK had been worth all the effort. 

A community worth bringing home 

I attended my first IENE conference in Prague in 2024. I'll be honest: when I saw the programme ran for 5 days, I was surprised. By the end of the week, I completely understood why. 

IENE brings together people working where infrastructure meets nature, from across Europe and beyond. Ecologists rarely find themselves in the same room as transport planners, engineers, economists, policymakers and infrastructure operators, yet all of them shape the landscapes we depend on. Surrounded by this international community, the field feels large and established. But back home in your day job, it can feel like a very small niche. 

I wanted UK colleagues to experience what I experienced in Prague, the realisation that a huge amount of knowledge and practical experience already exists. Across Europe, people are testing solutions, learning from what doesn't work and sharing those lessons. We don't always need another pilot project. Sometimes we simply need to learn from the people who have already done the work. 

That diversity of experience showed from the start. Our opening panel in Bristol, Green is Cheaper than Grey, led by Natural England's Oliver Harmar, brought developers, architects, government agencies and industry leaders together to challenge the idea that nature is an added cost. Building nature in from the outset can cut long-term costs, improve resilience and add wider social and environmental value. As panellist Louise Clarke from Berkeley Group said afterwards: "It was refreshing being on a panel and looking out and only recognising one face." 

That kind of joined-up conversation is exactly what Natural England's strategy, Recovering Nature for Growth, Health and Security, calls for. It recognises that resilient economies, healthy communities and critical infrastructure all depend on functioning natural systems, and that nature recovery can't be delivered in isolation. Bringing IENE to Bristol was a chance to learn from international experience and strengthen the partnerships we need. 

Why "the value of nature"? 

We deliberately chose the IENE 2026 theme to provoke debate. Some people hear The Value of Nature in Resilient Infrastructure and think of the services nature provides: trees cooling cities, wetlands reducing flood risk, healthy ecosystems helping infrastructure withstand a changing climate. Others think about economics. How do we account for nature in decisions without reducing it to a simple number, and make investment choices that respect ecological limits? 

Those questions ran through the week, explored in-depth by Erik Gómez-Baggethun, a leading figure in ecological economics and environmental governance during his keynote. There wasn't a single answer, but there was broad agreement that infrastructure, climate resilience and nature recovery can no longer be treated as separate conversations. 

Nature is infrastructure 

One of the strongest messages to emerge from the conference was the growing recognition that nature is critical infrastructure. Across the programme, speakers explored how healthy natural systems increase the resilience of transport networks and help deliver better outcomes for people and places. 

Reflecting on the discussions, Tony Juniper, Chair of Natural England, said: 

"One thing that came out loud and clear is how nature is infrastructure. Healthy blanket bogs are flood defences and sources of pure water, nature protects infrastructure, including roads and railways that would otherwise flood, and infrastructure can be built more quickly when nature is fully blended into construction plans, such as green bridges over trunk roads. The idea that nature and infrastructure are opposites is an idea well past its sell by date." 

That theme came up repeatedly. Speakers from across Europe, South America and beyond showed how green bridges, wildlife crossings, railway corridors and restored habitats are reconnecting fragmented landscapes. Long-term monitoring showed that well-designed crossings improve safety for both wildlife and people. When connectivity is designed in from the start, the benefits go far beyond just for biodiversity's sake. 

What we heard from the experts 

A keynote that stayed with me came from Manuela Panzacchi of the Norwegian Institute for Nature Research. Her modelling tools show how infrastructure, climate change and other human activity affect wildlife movement, and can test future scenarios to identify the most vulnerable corridors. Whether the discussion was roads, rail, power, ports or urban development, the same principles kept emerging: connectivity matters, ecological limits matter, and nature must be considered from the start. 

The policy session was equally thought-provoking. One talk on nature-positive procurement challenged us to build biodiversity into the business case much earlier, before designs are fixed and opportunities are lost. 

Another explored liability for wildlife-vehicle collisions across Europe, sparking a fascinating discussion with a colleague from National Highways. We reflected on the UK's limited roadkill data and how lessons from our European counterparts could help us understand the issue better and inform future action. 

Technology was another recurring theme, from AI-powered biodiversity monitoring and habitat mapping to collision prediction tools. It's no substitute for ecological expertise, but it is becoming a powerful tool for better-informed decisions. 

Seeing Bristol through new eyes 

On the Wednesday, delegates joined field trips across the West of England. I joined the Bristol Harbour boat trip and, despite living and working here, learned a huge amount about my own city. 

From the water, we passed SS Great Britain and Temple Meads, we saw floating ecosystems and waterfront regeneration transforming former industrial landscapes while protecting the green and blue spaces that make Bristol unique. It was a fitting illustration of the week's central message: with the right planning and ambition, nature and development can reinforce one another. 

Leaving a living legacy 

The Organising Committee didn't want the conference to disappear as soon as everyone boarded their trains and flights home. Throughout the week, native trees supplied by The Tree Council were displayed across the venue. They are now being planted during National Tree Week as part of the emerging Western Forest, helping create Pucklechurch Wood. Together, they will form the IENE 2026 Copps. 

I love the symbolism. For 30 years, IENE has been growing knowledge and partnerships across Europe, and now a small part of that story will literally keep growing in the landscape. 

Thirty years on, what next? 

The conference closed with reflections from Edgar van der Grift, one of IENE's founding members. From the first IENE conference welcoming less than 100 people from 20 countries to nearly 300 delegates from more than 40 countries in Bristol. Edgar observed that, after 30 years, the ecological viability of IENE itself appeared to be in very healthy condition. 

I couldn't agree more. New leadership, a renewed board and a new generation of members bring challenges, but also opportunities. What hasn't changed is the need for the work. 

Bristol wasn't a conclusion. It was the next step in putting nature and people at the heart of infrastructure thinking. For Natural England, that's why hosting IENE 2026 mattered. If we're serious about recovering nature for growth, health and security, learning from one another and working beyond traditional boundaries will be essential. 

Get involved 

If your work or interests sit where infrastructure, transport and nature meet, IENE is a fantastic community to be part of. Find out more at iene.info.

entry.title: Working together sustains Hen Harrier numbers in 2026
entry.summary: By Matt Heard, National Delivery Director Hen Harriers are one of the UK’s most distinctive birds of prey and, after decades of decline, have gradually returned to northern England as their population has recovered. Natural England and its partners are …
entry.content:
By Matt Heard, National Delivery Director

Hen Harriers are one of the UK’s most distinctive birds of prey and, after decades of decline, have gradually returned to northern England as their population has recovered. Natural England and its partners are working to support this recovery through the Joint Action Plan, helping to balance conservation with wider land management priorities. Annual monitoring shows a long-term positive trend, with efforts focused on tracking breeding success across England. This blog gives the latest figures for 2026. 

Numbers of nesting Hen Harriers in England increased in 2026, according to data collected by Natural England, RSPB and partners. 

Hen Harriers are a charismatic yet elusive bird of prey species, at home on upland moorland landscapes in the UK. Once reduced to just a few isolated pockets, Hen Harriers have spread from Scotland and returned to the north of England as their numbers have gradually recovered over the past few decades. 

Conflicting land management priorities have slowed their recovery, but Natural England and partners have been working to secure their future in England through cooperation under the Joint action plan to increase the English hen harrier population, which was published by Defra in 2016.  

Securing a future for the Hen Harrier in England is one of the ways in which Natural England is working to deliver our latest strategy: Recovering Nature for Growth, Health and Security, strengthening the resilience of England's ecosystems and the services they provide through the protection and recovery of key ecosystem components, including species like the Hen Harrier. 

Monitoring the recovery of hen harriers in England

As part of the Joint Action Plan, Natural England and partners including the RSPB and raptor monitoring groups collect data on the number of breeding Hen Harriers each year, and, where possible, the number of chicks that successfully fledge each year. It is unlikely that all the breeding Hen Harriers in England are counted, but great effort is made to work with landowners and managers to ensure as many as possible are added to the records to give the best estimate each year. While the data collected by Natural England and partners does not always show an increase on the preceding year, the overall trend of the species' population has shown much growth on a longer timescale, in both number and distribution. Previous annual reporting on the national population, published by Natural England, can be seen here: 2025, 2024, 2023, 2022. 

Breeding figures and regional breakdown

In 2026, Natural England, RSPB and partners recorded a total of 45 breeding attempts in England (39 in 2025), of which 33 were successful (33 in 2025), fledging 112 chicks (106 in 2025). This gives an average of 3.4 chicks per successful nest (3.2 in 2025).   

We recorded 1 second breeding attempt in 2026. Therefore, it is estimated that there was a minimum of 44 breeding females in England (39 in 2025).

Trends in Hen Harrier numbers  

The overall figures show a steady increase in breeding attempts by Hen Harriers over the past 2 years, following a crash in 2024. Anecdotal observations by field staff reported an increase in the availability of prey items (including voles) in 2026, which is likely to have contributed to this increase. However, this was not the case in all areas and a number of factors will also have played an influential role. Annual population fluctuations are to be expected for any species of wild animal, but while the national population remains so small the ability for a population to recover from a decline is significantly reduced. This highlights the need for continued effort to increase the number of Hen Harriers in England and improve their resilience to bounce back from poorer breeding years, which can result from variables such as prey and habitat availability, which may in turn be affected by land management regimes and a changing climate. 

This year only 9 of the 45 recorded breeding attempts were made on moors managed for grouse in England, with the remainder across other moorland and water catchment locations (including but not limited to nature reserves). The relatively small number of breeding attempts on grouse moors could be due to the reduced monitoring of grouse moors in 2026 in comparison to previous years. Our monitoring team would welcome the opportunity to work with more moorland owners and agree access and monitoring agreements, with the aim of getting a more complete picture of Hen Harrier numbers. 

Working with partners is key  

We are grateful for the efforts of our partners to monitor, protect and manage Hen Harrier nests and breeding habitats. We work closely with RSPB staff who record the nesting attempts on RSPB reserves, and on the United Utilities Estate in Bowland. We are also grateful for the contributions of volunteer Raptor Study Groups and Natural England volunteers to nest monitoring, and to landowners and agencies including Forestry England, National Parks, National Landscapes, the National Trust, NatureScot and Natural Resources Wales.  Natural England field staff lead on liaison with privately-owned grouse shooting estates, and we extend our gratitude to those land managers who are encouraging Hen Harriers to nest successfully alongside their wider estate management for grouse and other wildlife.  

2026 marks 30 years of consolidated data for Hen Harrier breeding activity in England. Natural England is committed to recovering nature, and the Hen Harrier is one example of how long-term dedication can have real meaningful impact for species and landscapes.  

We are committed to continue to work with all partners and communities to improve the long-term recovery of Hen Harriers.

entry.title: My first day at Natural England: sustainable development for people and nature
entry.summary: In this post, new Natural England Chief Executive, Neil Hornby, reflects on his first day at Natural England and his ambitions for the organisation.
entry.content:
Reflections from Neil Hornby, Chief Executive of Natural England 

In this blog, Neil Hornby marks their first day as Chief Executive of Natural England with a visit to Kent to see how housing development and nature recovery can work hand in hand. Reflecting on a new Operational Statement that lets Natural England focus its planning advice where it matters most, and on early progress through the Nature Restoration Fund and the Norfolk Environmental Delivery Plan, Neil sets out a vision for an organisation that is ambitious for nature, pragmatic in its approach, and genuinely collaborative with developers, farmers and communities alike.

I wanted my first day as Chief Executive of Natural England to begin not behind a desk, but out on the ground with colleagues and partners. So today I will visit Kent to meet with Barratt Redrow and see their Conningbrook development – where I will see first-hand how homes, infrastructure and nature recovery can be planned and delivered together. I will also visit a partner’s environmental works, to look at how mitigation for nutrient pollution can be developed. 

As Chief Executive, I want Natural England to be ambitious in its efforts to recover nature and be straightforward in the way it works: an organisation that protects and restores nature, uses the best available science and evidence, listens to its customers and partners and delivers effectively. I don’t want us to just be known for identifying environmental risks and issues, but for helping people find solutions that are a win-win for nature and people. 

 I know I am stepping into a critically important role at a vital time. As we face the twin crises of biodiversity loss and climate change - in one of the most nature-depleted countries in the world - our work to recover nature and improve access to it has never been more important or more urgent.  

Too much of the wildlife that inspired my love of nature as a child has been lost and too many people have become disconnected from the natural world. And that’s why I am committed to this important task. 

At Conningbrook, I will see a growing community alongside a 3.2 hectare nutrient mitigation wetland. The site is a practical example of development working with nature: early engagement from both the developer and our teams, a clear understanding of environmental pressures and partnership working have helped create space for new homes, green space and addressed impacts on the internationally important Stodmarsh wetland site. 

A clear purpose and a focused way of working 

That is the approach I want us to build on. Today, Natural England are also publishing a new Operational Statement allowing us to prioritise our planning advice more strategically to have the greatest impact for nature and people. This follows recent changes in the Planning and Infrastructure Act 2025.  

Previously, Natural England was required to provide advice on every request relating to development under the Town and Country Planning Act. This meant specialist expertise was spread across a high volume of consultations, including routine cases where established guidance already existed. The amended duty brings our role more closely in line with other statutory consultees. 

In practice, this means engaging earlier with local authorities in developing plans and strategic solutions, providing clearer standing advice, standard guidance and evidence for routine or lower-risk proposals, and reserving bespoke input for the most complex cases and those presenting the greatest risks or opportunities for nature.  This approach is intended to provide greater certainty and consistency for local planning authorities and developers while ensuring specialist advice is focused where it can add the greatest value for nature and people. 

Statutory consultation requirements remain unchanged, as do the protections for important habitats, species and designated sites. We will continue to fulfil our legal responsibilities and provide responses where planning and environmental legislation requires it.  

The new approach will be carefully introduced through a phased approach with partners.  

From site-by-site mitigation to work at scale 

This focus on strategic engagement and larger scale solutions is already reflected in our work on the Nature Restoration Fund, where developers can make a levy payment towards a coordinated programme of conservation measures, rather than commissioning fragmented mitigation site by site.  

Our first draft Environmental Delivery Plan for Norfolk, published for consultation in the last fortnight, builds on our previous work on providing strategic solutions to tackle the impacts of pollution and support the recovery of protected species.  

The first plan is intended to help unlock up to 15,780 homes while raising more than £30 million for large-scale improvements to rivers and wetlands, including the Norfolk Broads. We welcome your feedback on this plan as we seek to roll out this important scheme.  

My vision for Natural England 

Natural England’s core purpose - to achieve nature recovery - is clear and non-negotiable. I’m clear that our strategy, Recovering Nature for Growth, Health and Security, provides the blueprint for the outcomes we seek and how we will achieve them. We must deliver successful nature recovery at scale and across all parts of our country. This will mean developing new approaches and building strong partnerships to ensure that nature’s essential contribution to our economy, health and national security is fully valued.  

I want to be relentlessly focused on how Natural England can deliver for nature in a way that is customer focused, collaborative and pragmatic. That means making our advice timely and practical, setting expectations clearly and focusing our expertise where it can achieve the greatest impact. And it means Natural England working in genuine partnership with infrastructure developers, housebuilders, farmers, land managers, businesses, local authorities and communities to deliver shared objectives on growth, clean energy, food security, health and nature recovery together.  

Over the coming weeks and months, I look forward to hearing from colleagues, customers and partners about our work together and to exploring opportunities to do more to deliver for people and nature.

entry.title: SSSIs: A Golden Thread Through My Career
entry.summary: In this blog, Marian Spain reflects on Sites of Special Scientific Interest (SSSIs) as a golden thread through her time as Chief Executive of Natural England. Highlighting Dearne Valley Wetlands, West Penwith Moors and Downs, and Teesmouth and Cleveland Coast, Marian shows how SSSIs have evolved from academic curiosities into the backbone of nature recovery, …
entry.content:
By Marian Spain, CEO of Natural England

In this blog, Marian Spain reflects on Sites of Special Scientific Interest (SSSIs) as a golden thread through her time as Chief Executive of Natural England. Highlighting Dearne Valley Wetlands, West Penwith Moors and Downs, and Teesmouth and Cleveland Coast, Marian shows how SSSIs have evolved from academic curiosities into the backbone of nature recovery, and argues that successful designation depends on partnership, communication and trust with the landowners and communities who care for these special places.

As I prepare to leave Natural England after 8 years as Chief Executive, I have been reflecting on the themes that have run consistently through my career in nature conservation.

One of those is protecting our most special places and most precious wildlife and geology, including by designating Sites of Special Scientific Interest (SSSI). One of the first things I did when I became CEO was designate the Down Farm SSSI and I’m delighted then that one of the last things I have done is agree a new programme of sites being considered for designation in the next 3 years, together with a new approach to working with our stakeholders as we consider these. We’ll be publishing that on GOV.UK very soon.

SSSIs are among the most powerful tools we have to recognise and protect the very best of England's wildlife, habitats and geology, and we don’t undertake them lightly: they have a big impact (including sometimes restricting what a landowner can and can’t do) and need a very high level of scientific and legal proof to merit such significant protection. Currently we have 4,128, making up 8% of England’s land area.

They celebrate places that are nationally important for nature, while helping to secure the benefits that healthy natural systems provide to society. They protect some of our most precious species and habitats and geology as the very best of a wide range of landscapes and seascapes in cities, countryside and the coast. And they also help deliver cleaner rivers, healthier soils, carbon storage, flood resilience and opportunities for people to experience nature close to home. 

SSSIs are and have always been about much more than just designation to protect wildlife and habitats. They represent our nation’s commitment to recognising what is special, understanding why it matters, and ensuring it can thrive for future generations.

Historically, they were often viewed primarily as representative examples for academic study. Increasingly, we now recognise them as the foundations of nature recovery. They are the places where our most valuable wildlife and habitats persist and they are also the places from which nature can recover and spread across wider landscapes. They are the backbone of nature recovery, the reservoirs of biodiversity that help reconnect fragmented habitats and support thriving ecosystems for the future. 

Natural England is now taking a renewed approach to SSSI designation. We have strengthened the way we make decisions, improved planning and prioritisation, reconsidered the tasks and the resources to carry out designation projects, including spending enough time with those affected and those who will benefit to explain what will happen and why. That means we have also developed a more certain and more strategic programme for future designations. We are prioritising sites based on their contribution to nature recovery, the protection of vulnerable habitats and species, and the wider benefits they provide for society, with a programme phased to bring forward those which are closest to being able to be delivered, allowing us to focus on embedding our new ways of working.

During my time as Chief Executive, I have been proud to see important places be designated to protect and conserve the wildlife and habitats that call these places home. 

In South Yorkshire, the notification of Dearne Valley Wetlands as a new SSSI, recognised a remarkable landscape where nature has flourished alongside the legacy of industrial change. Its nationally important bird populations and wetland habitats demonstrate how nature recovery can transform places, delivering benefits not only for wildlife but also for local communities through access to nature and flood resilience. 

In Cornwall, the confirmation of West Penwith Moors and Downs as a SSSI protected more than 3,000 hectares of nationally important habitats and species. The designation recognised not only the extraordinary wildlife of the area but also the centuries of farming and land management that helped shape its distinctive character. 

During my time at Natural England, the importance of protecting the wildlife and geology interest of Teesmouth and Cleveland Coast SSSI has also become a powerful example of how we must navigate the relationship between nature recovery and development. Its story illustrates one of the defining challenges of how we recover nature while also meeting society's need for homes, infrastructure and economic growth.

Too often these objectives are presented as opposing choices. England needs new homes, new infrastructure and new investment. But we also need thriving wildlife, resilient ecosystems and access to nature. The challenge is not whether we choose nature or development, but how we plan, design and invest so that both can succeed, sites such as Teesmouth and Cleveland Coast, reinforce the importance of identifying opportunities where sustainable development can proceed while contributing positively to nature recovery. SSSIs don’t stop economic activity happening – be that farming, development or natural resource use, but they make sure that for these very special places nature is given a “seat at the table” when decisions are made about land use.

One of the most important lessons I have learned throughout my career is that nature recovery is not something that can be delivered to people. It is something that must be achieved with people.

The success of any SSSI ultimately depends on the people who own, manage and care for the land. Farmers, commoners, landowners, conservation organisations and local communities are not simply stakeholders in these places; they are central to their future.

That is why I am particularly pleased that Natural England's renewed approach to SSSI designation places such emphasis on partnership, communication and engagement. Alongside strengthening our internal processes, we have recognised the importance of working more closely with landowners and local communities from the outset, ensuring that people understand both the reasons for designation and the opportunities that can follow from it, as well as whether it will mean any limits on how land is managed in the future. We want designation to be something that is developed with people, and that landowners can be proud of, not something that feels as though it is being done to them. 

Sometimes designation discussions can create uncertainty and concern. People understandably want to know what designation means for their businesses, their communities and the places they care about. We have learned that clear communication, transparency and early engagement are essential. Listening to concerns, explaining the evidence, and working through challenges together leads to better outcomes for everyone.

Recent experience has highlighted both the strength of feeling people have for the landscapes they manage and the importance of maintaining an open and constructive dialogue throughout the designation process. Those experiences have helped shape our future approach, placing greater emphasis on communication, stakeholder engagement and long-term relationships with those who manage these special places. The most effective conservation does not happen when change is perceived as something being imposed. It happens when people share an understanding of what makes a place special, why it matters, and how protecting and enhancing it can benefit both nature and society.

That is what Natural England is committed to do, in our mission of building partnerships for nature’s recovery. And as our strategy says, recovering nature - including by making sure wildlife is thriving in protected sites - in ways that support growth, health and security.

entry.title: Marian Spain - from first conversations to Landscape Recovery: a career in the field
entry.summary: In this blog, Marian Spain reflects on Landscape Recovery, the ambitious agri-environment scheme uniting farmers, NGOs and investors across whole landscapes for 20-year commitments. Highlighting projects like Upper Duddon, Boothby and Evenlode, Marian shows how nature restoration and farm resilience combine to deliver food security, climate benefits and thriving rural communities.
entry.content:
By Marian Spain, CEO of Natural England

In this blog, Marian Spain reflects on Landscape Recovery, the ambitious agri-environment scheme uniting farmers, NGOs and investors across whole landscapes for 20-year commitments. Highlighting projects like Upper Duddon, Boothby and Evenlode, Marian shows how nature restoration and farm resilience combine to deliver food security, climate benefits and thriving rural communities.

I started my career on the very first agri-environment schemes, working with farmers in East Anglia to agree the small, practical changes that could bring nature back to their land. I spent years having those conversations, and what struck me most was how many farmers wanted to see more wildlife on their land. That is still important to many farmers, but I am also increasingly struck by how many farmers now see nature as a vital part of their business. Better soil health, more pollinators, shade from trees, more water and wetlands all help make farms more resilient and so contribute to food security, and the security of individual businesses.

The importance of that connection between farming and nature has never left me. It's why, as I look back over my career, I feel such pride that it now includes the development of the most ambitious agri-environment scheme we've ever attempted: Landscape Recovery.

Landscape Recovery is built on a simple idea: that nature and farm resilience are two sides of the same coin. It asks farmers, landowners and their partners to think bigger, working across whole landscapes rather than single fields, and to commit for the long term, for 20 years or more, so that changes can take root across a generation rather than a single business cycle. It also asks projects to bring in private finance alongside public funding, and to build real partnerships with the communities who live and work in these landscapes. In doing so, it answers a call made over a decade ago by Sir John Lawton for habitats that are bigger, better, and more joined up.

None of this happens through one organisation alone. Landscape Recovery is a genuinely joint endeavour, delivered with Defra, the Environment Agency and the Forestry Commission and of course with all of the partners  - farmers, local authorities, environmental NGOs, National Parks and National Landscapes - involved in the projects, and I want to thank everyone who has helped shape this scheme from the ground up.

Real progress, on the ground takes time – but the outcomes for the nation are huge

I know that Landscape Recovery can sometimes seem slow to develop – from initial ideas to things happening on the ground takes 2-3 years.  Developing a project of this scale, across multiple landholdings, with farmers, tenants, environmental organisations and private investors all working towards a shared plan, does takes time. And a lot of hard work from all involved. It has to. We're asking projects to build something robust enough to last two decades and deliver genuine value for public money, and that means getting the foundations right before work starts.

Results are coming through

Since the first round opened in 2022, 56 projects have come through our two pilot rounds developing proposals across more than 250,000 ha.  This has involved over 1,000 farmers and land managers who have taken part in developing this scheme alongside environmental NGOs, academics and private finance partners. Three projects are now delivering for nature across c6,700ha, and more will be underway before the year is out, which together could mean a total of more than 20,000 ha in delivery contributing to nature recovery, climate resilience and farm sustainability.

One of those is the Upper Duddon Landscape Recovery Project in South-West Cumbria which began delivery in July 2025 across roughly 2,800 hectares of upland farming country. Led by the University of Leeds, it brings tenant farmers, landowners and environmental partners together to protect fell farming traditions while restoring the River Duddon and its tributaries, improving water quality, reducing flood risk downstream, and creating jobs and volunteering opportunities for the local community.

I recently had the pleasure of celebrating this milestone with the Duddon team, and I heard two things from the farmers I met:

“The valley is coming back to life” - more jobs, more people, more activity, more nature; and “the scheme gives us a future” - the certainty of 20 years income means farmers and their successors can be confident to keep investing in their business and their family’s livelihoods.  That, for me, captures exactly what this scheme is about.

Alongside Duddon, the Boothby Landscape Recovery Project is an ambitious nature recovery and river restoration project in Lincolnshire, led by Nattergal covering over 600 hectares of land.  The project combines public and private investment to deliver long-term biodiversity recovery, carbon storage and flood resilience and is now well into implementation, signing its agreement in June 2025.

The Evenlode Landscape Recovery Project, is a farmer-led landscape restoration initiative across the Evenlode catchment in the Cotswolds, aiming to improve river health, biodiversity, flood resilience and sustainable farming across more than 3,000 hectares. It is led by the North East Cotswold Farmer Cluster CIC (NECFC) and involves over 50 farmers and land managers working collaboratively to deliver long-term environmental recovery.  I'm delighted to see it progressing alongside our other pioneering projects.

What we're learning from Landscape Recovery

For farmers considering their own path, the principles behind LR translate directly into farm-level benefits: restoring native habitats brings back pollinators and natural pest control, healthier soils support better yields, and re-meandering rivers or restoring wetlands can keep nutrients on your land and reduce flood risk. Entering an LR project also means working with your neighbours, with a local project manager to manage the scheme on behalf of everybody (and help with the paperwork!)  and with people who understand your local landscape and who tailor the project to it. You will also be contributing for the nation to ensure food security, climate resilience and more nature for everybody’s wellbeing.

Thank you to all our partners

As Chief Executive, I have the responsibility of signing off each LR grant agreement, and I don't take that lightly. Every signature represents years of work by landowners, tenants, communities and partners to agree a shared vision and proof it can deliver.

To everyone who took part in rounds one and two, the farmers and tenant farmers, environmental NGOs, academics, private finance partners and more, thank you.

Your patience and ambition are spearheading and building something genuinely new for the benefit of your land and communities.

Let's continue to drive this ambition forward.

Find out more:

Find out more about Landscape Recovery and its ongoing projects by searching "Landscape Recovery" on the Defra Farming Blog.
